solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Judgment after temper's raised

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means the word is read upwards, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: temper means mood, as in being in a bad mood

explanation.surface: A verdict delivered only once someone has lost their temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns MOOD upwards in this down entry, giving DOOM.
explanation.definitionFit: Doom is fate or a final verdict, as in the Day of Judgment or Doomsday.

clue.text: Defensive batsman, one playing for time with one wicket in hand

indicators.note: held in hand means the following pieces are gripped inside the word for a time-waster

parts.note: a staller is someone who delays to gain time
taken as written
W is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for wicket

explanation.surface: A cricketer digs in to save the match with only the last wicket left.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture of a last-wicket stand is a mirage; 'one playing for time' is a separate piece, not part of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, a stolid player who blocks every ball rather than scoring runs is called this.

clue.text: Small convenient drink

parts.note: S is the usual abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
handy means convenient or within easy reach

explanation.surface: A small drink that is easy to come by.
explanation.definitionFit: Shandy is a British drink of beer mixed with lemonade, a light pub drink.

clue.text: Grandeur of railways in USA

indicators.note: railways are placed in the middle of the word for USA, a container

parts.note: the USA is the States, short for the United States
lines are railway routes, as in branch lines

explanation.surface: Admiring the impressive scale of American railroads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'railways' suggests a rail network, but the railway word is just lines placed inside the country's short name.
explanation.definitionFit: Stateliness is dignified magnificence, a near synonym of grandeur.

clue.text: Spies a convenience

parts.note: in Britain a public convenience is a toilet, and the gents is the men's toilet

explanation.surface: Secret agents meeting at a public lavatory.
explanation.walkthrough: Convenience is a British euphemism for a public toilet; the GENTS is the men's one.
explanation.definitionFit: Agents are those who gather secret intelligence, so spies is a straight synonym.

clue.text: Lower classes intended resistance

parts.note: D and E are the lowest grades in the British social classification scale
one's intended is one's fiancé, the person one plans to marry

explanation.surface: The working classes meant to put up opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: British market research grades society A, B, C1, C2, D, E, so the lower classes are D and E; 'intended' is a noun, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Defiance is open refusal to obey, a form of resistance.

clue.text: Ostentation shown by British page

parts.note: Pom is Australian slang for a British person

explanation.surface: A display of showiness by a British pageboy.
explanation.walkthrough: POM is Australian and New Zealand slang for a Briton.
explanation.definitionFit: Pomp is ceremonial splendour or showy display, which is what ostentation means.

clue.text: Factory to design vintage model of car

parts.note: to plan something is to design it
the Model T was Ford's famous early car

explanation.surface: A works set up to design classic cars.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ford Model T, built from 1908, gives the single letter T.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant is an industrial works or manufacturing site, the same thing as a factory.

clue.text: Test to following golden rule

parts.note: the MOT is the annual roadworthiness test for British cars

explanation.surface: A test followed by a guiding principle.
explanation.walkthrough: The MOT is the annual safety test British cars must pass; 'following' is a link setting the pieces in order.
explanation.definitionFit: A motto is a short guiding maxim, and a golden rule is a basic principle to live by.

clue.text: Crew perhaps get tips from Oxford, Cambridge teams entering Thames

indicators.note: the tips are the front ends of each following word, so their initials are taken

explanation.surface: Boat race crews from the two universities take to the Thames.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the Boat Race; an eight-person rowing crew is a group of eight, hence 'perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: A rowing eight is one example of a group of eight, signalled by 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Star Scottish footballer gets red card

definitions.meaning: an ace is a star, and Hearts (Heart of Midlothian) is an Edinburgh football club, so its best player
a playing card of the hearts suit, which is printed red

explanation.surface: A top Scottish player is sent off.
explanation.walkthrough: Hearts is an Edinburgh football club; 'red card' wants to be a sending-off but is a playing card in a red suit.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearts are a red suit in a pack, so the ace of that suit is a red card.

clue.text: Olympic winner to catch impressionist

parts.note: Mo Farah, the British runner, won Olympic gold medals
to net something is to catch it, as with a fish

explanation.surface: An Olympic champion manages to catch a mimic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'impressionist' suggests a mimic, but it is the French painter Claude Monet.
explanation.definitionFit: Claude Monet founded French Impressionism, the painting movement named after his work.

clue.text: Former wife's custom is being sent abroad

parts.note: an ex is a former wife or partner
a tradition is a long-standing custom

explanation.surface: An ex-wife's habit of moving overseas.
explanation.definitionFit: Extradition is the formal handing over of a suspect to another country, which is being sent abroad.

clue.text: In the present month, all fellows will take time setting up in office

parts.note: inst., short for instant, means of the current month in old letter-writing
taken as written
men are fellows

explanation.surface: This month everyone will take time to move into the new office.
explanation.walkthrough: INST (instant) is old business-letter shorthand for this month, as in 'yours of the 5th inst.'
explanation.definitionFit: Installment, also spelt installation, is the formal induction of someone into an office.

clue.text: Press has short article taking popular line during Cold War

parts.note: to iron clothes is to press them
curt means short or abrupt
a is the indefinite article
in means popular or fashionable

explanation.surface: A newspaper runs a brief piece toeing the popular line in the Cold War.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' looks like the newspapers but is the verb meaning to iron.
explanation.definitionFit: The dividing boundary between Soviet and Western Europe during the Cold War was known by this name.

clue.text: Get snug in finest leather

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of letters across these two words

explanation.surface: Snuggling into the best leather.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs from finEST LEather... starting at the N of finest.
explanation.definitionFit: To nestle is to settle comfortably and cosily, which is to get snug.

clue.text: It's puzzling to put together dances with a wife

parts.note: jigs are lively folk dances

explanation.surface: Combining lively dances with a wife is baffling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put together' reads as joining the pieces, but it belongs to the definition: a picture puzzle that is assembled.
explanation.definitionFit: A jigsaw is a picture puzzle that has to be assembled from interlocking pieces.

clue.text: Type inclined to have attraction to adventurous girl mostly

parts.note: it is old slang for sex appeal or charm

indicators.note: mostly means most of the word, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: Alice has adventures in Wonderland in Lewis Carroll's story

explanation.surface: Someone inclined to fancy a daring girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' drops the last letter of ALICE to give ALIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Italic type is a typeface whose letters slope to the right.

clue.text: Taking steamship round Channel Islands explorer returned in cutter

indicators.note: the steamship letters go round the following pieces, enclosing them
returned means the explorer's name is read backwards

parts.note: James Clark Ross was a polar explorer

explanation.surface: A steamer passes the Channel Islands as an explorer comes home aboard a revenue cutter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns the explorer's name backwards. 'cutter' suggests a boat, fitting the steamship picture, but means a cutting tool.
explanation.definitionFit: Scissors are a cutting implement, so they are literally a cutter.

clue.text: Redraft in coarse outline

indicators.note: to redraft is to write again, so the letters are rewritten in a new order

explanation.surface: Revising a rough draft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Redraft' rearranges the eight letters of IN COARSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A scenario is an outline of a plot or a sketch of possible events.

clue.text: Saint's given foreign church prominence

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for saint
alien means foreign
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A saint gains standing in an overseas church.
explanation.walkthrough: CE stands for the Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Salience means the quality of standing out, the same as prominence.

clue.text: Revoke excluding husband from part of church

indicators.note: excluding means a letter is left out of the word for part of a church

parts.note: the chancel is the part of a church near the altar

explanation.surface: Annulling a marriage by keeping the husband out of the chancel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excluding husband' removes H from CHANCEL.
explanation.definitionFit: To cancel something is to annul or withdraw it, which is to revoke it.

clue.text: Box with 'far, far better' character

definitions.meaning: Sydney ... in Dickens's A Tale of Two Cities says 'It is a far, far better thing that I do'

explanation.surface: A box carrying a famous literary quotation.
explanation.walkthrough: Sydney Carton speaks the famous 'far, far better thing' line before the guillotine in Dickens's A Tale of Two Cities.
explanation.definitionFit: A carton is a cardboard container, and Carton is also the Dickens hero.

clue.text: How Oliver was portrayed in battle, unlikely to hold beach

parts.note: war is a battle

indicators.note: the word for unlikely holds the beach word inside it

parts.note: tall, as in a tall story, means unlikely or hard to believe
sand covers a beach

explanation.surface: A soldier in battle hardly expected to hold the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver Cromwell told his painter to show him 'warts and all', blemishes included; 'Oliver' wants to be Dickens's Twist.
explanation.definitionFit: Cromwell asked to be painted with every blemish shown, giving the idiom for honest portrayal.

clue.text: Friendship as disaster spared California

indicators.note: spared means the word for disaster goes without the named letters

parts.note: a calamity is a disaster

explanation.surface: Friendship survives because California escaped catastrophe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spared California' removes CAL from CALAMITY.
explanation.definitionFit: Amity is friendly relations or goodwill, a synonym of friendship.

clue.text: Coach some coaches

definitions.meaning: to coach is to instruct or drill
a line of railway carriages, which are called coaches

explanation.surface: A coach on a coach outing.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'Coach' is a verb; the second is railway carriages.
explanation.definitionFit: To train is to coach, and a train is a set of linked carriages.

clue.text: One getting flame to marry

definitions.meaning: a small stick struck to produce a flame

explanation.surface: A lover with an old flame ready to wed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flame' suggests a sweetheart, but it is a literal fire.
explanation.definitionFit: A match is struck to give a flame, and to match people is to pair them in marriage.

clue.text: Take note of that man Miliband

parts.note: he means that man
Ed Miliband is a British Labour politician, former party leader

explanation.surface: Pay attention to that politician Miliband.
explanation.walkthrough: Ed Miliband led the British Labour Party from 2010 to 2015.
explanation.definitionFit: To heed is to pay attention to or take notice of.

clue.text: Dressing, being given attire in new fashion

indicators.note: the letters are made over in a new style, a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Dressing up in new clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in new fashion' rearranges GIVEN and ATTIRE; 'Dressing' suggests clothes but is a salad dressing.
explanation.definitionFit: Vinaigrette is a salad dressing of oil and vinegar.

clue.text: Innocent one in body of church

indicators.note: one is placed inside the body of church

parts.note: the nave is the main body of a church
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An innocent person standing in the nave.
explanation.walkthrough: I goes inside NAVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Naive means unworldly or guileless, as innocent can.

clue.text: Boy dashed round yard

indicators.note: round means the word for dashed goes around the next piece

parts.note: ran means dashed

explanation.surface: A boy sprinted around the yard.
explanation.walkthrough: RAN goes round Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Ryan is a boy's first name, giving a male name for the definition.

clue.text: One stinging nettle finally confused with thorn

indicators.note: confused means the combined letters are jumbled
finally takes the closing letter of the word nettle

explanation.surface: A nettle and a thorn mixed up as stinging plants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' gives E from nettle, and 'confused' mixes E with THORN; nettle and thorn suggest plants, not an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: A hornet is a large wasp that delivers a painful sting.
